current_example.title: Example: Solving Natural Logarithmic Equations by Combining Logarithmic Terms

q-19175.name: Question 1
q-19175.worked_solution:
To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The logarithm is a natural logarithm, which means its base is $e.$ So, we use a base of $e$ for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x) & =5 \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)} & ={e}^{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)}=5x.$ 

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}5x & ={e}^{5} \\ x & =\frac{1}{5}{e}^{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-19175.html:
Question 1
?

Find x such that ln⁡(5x)=5.

a
5e5
b
15e5
c
e1/5
d
e5
e
125e5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The logarithm is a natural logarithm, which means its base is e. So, we use a base of e for the exponentiation as well:

ln⁡(5x)=5eln⁡(5x)=e5

Since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get eln⁡(5x)=5x.

Therefore,

5x=e5x=15e5.

q-19181.name: Question 2
q-19181.worked_solution:
To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The logarithm is a natural logarithm, which means its base is $e.$ So, we use a base of $e$ for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{3}) & =3 \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x/3)} & ={e}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x/3)}=\frac{x}{3}.$ 

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{3} & ={e}^{3} \\ x & =3{e}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Find the exact solution to ln⁡(x3)=3.

a
x=3e3
b
x=e
c
x=2e3
d
x=3−e3
e
x=e3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The logarithm is a natural logarithm, which means its base is e. So, we use a base of e for the exponentiation as well:

ln⁡(x3)=3eln⁡(x/3)=e3

Since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get eln⁡(x/3)=x3.

Therefore, x3=e3x=3e3

q-79393.name: Question 3
q-79393.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange our equation to isolate the logarithmic term, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-5x)+3 & =9 \\ 2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-5x) & =6 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(1-5x) & =3\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The logarithm is a natural logarithm, which means its base is $e.$ So, we use a base of $e$ for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-5x) & =3 \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-5x)} & ={e}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-5x)}=1-5x.$ 

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}1-5x & ={e}^{3} \\ -5x & ={e}^{3}-1 \\ x & =\frac{{e}^{3}-1}{-5} \\ x & =\frac{1-{e}^{3}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

2ln⁡(1−5x)+3=92ln⁡(1−5x)=6ln⁡(1−5x)=3

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The logarithm is a natural logarithm, which means its base is e. So, we use a base of e for the exponentiation as well:

ln⁡(1−5x)=3eln⁡(1−5x)=e3

Since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get eln⁡(1−5x)=1−5x.

Therefore,

1−5x=e3−5x=e3−1x=e3−1−5x=1−e35.

q-110776.name: Question 4
q-110776.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange our equation to isolate the logarithmic term, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+1 & =2 \\ 2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1) & =1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1) & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The logarithm is a natural logarithm, which means its base is $e.$ So, we use a base of $e$ for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1) & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)} & ={e}^{1/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)}=x+1.$ 

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & ={e}^{1/2} \\ x+1 & =\sqrt{e} \\ x & =\sqrt{e}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

q-7940.name: Question 5
q-7940.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange our equation to isolate the logarithmic term, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3-7x)+8 & =24 \\ 4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3-7x) & =16 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(3-7x) & =4\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The logarithm is a natural logarithm, which means its base is $e.$ So, we use a base of $e$ for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3-7x) & =4 \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3-7x)} & ={e}^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3-7x)}=3-7x.$ 

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}3-7x & ={e}^{4} \\ -7x & ={e}^{4}-3 \\ x & =\frac{{e}^{4}-3}{-7} \\ x & =\frac{3-{e}^{4}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-66748.name: Question 6
q-66748.problem: If $\operatorname{ln}⁡x=1-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x$, then what is the value of  $x?$
q-66748.worked_solution:
First, we simplify our equation by collecting the like logarithmic terms, and isolating the logarithm, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡x & =1-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡x+2\operatorname{ln}⁡x & =1 \\ (1+2)\operatorname{ln}⁡x & =1 \\ 3\operatorname{ln}⁡x & =1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡x & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The logarithm is a natural logarithm, which means its base is $e.$ So, we use a base of $e$ for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡x & =\frac{1}{3} \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} & ={e}^{1/3}\end{aligned}
$$

Since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=x.$ 

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={e}^{1/3} \\ x & =\sqrt[3]{e}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-110778.worked_solution:
First, we simplify our equation by collecting the like logarithmic terms, and isolating the logarithm, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+5\operatorname{ln}⁡x & =7 \\ (2+5)\operatorname{ln}⁡x & =7 \\ 7\operatorname{ln}⁡x & =7 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡x & =\frac{7}{7} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The logarithm is a natural logarithm, which means its base is $e.$ So, we use a base of $e$ for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡x & =1 \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} & ={e}^{1}\end{aligned}
$$

Since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=x.$ 

Therefore, $x=e.$
